MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
significant popularity in recent years. Despite its success, MongoDB's
transactional functionality remains poorly understood, particularly in regards
to its default isolation level, which is currently set to "session" and
equivalent to linearizability. In the context of distributed MongoDB, with its
default configuration utilizing three nodes, research aims to explore the
following areas: validating the integrity of individual transactions through
validation functions, and verifying the consistency of data across transactions
through integrity rules. This study outlines a method to extract the precise
conditions under which transactions are considered valid and integral in
distributed MongoDB. Although previously existing approaches could validate the
linearizability of MongoDB's sessions, they fell short in validating the
integral nature of individual transactions. In contrast, our proposed framework
validates not only the sessions but also individual transactions in MongoDB,
with the additional benefit of being compatible with the standard specification
format. In the course of this research, we discovered that MongoDB's
transactional integrity can be complicated by certain configuration options,
with one example being the generation of random OAuth access token values.
Our research culminates in the creation of an executable specification that
confirms the distribution of MongoDB (version 4.4) enforcing the default
isolation level of linearizability, with all its features, across various
scenarios. Our findings, available for further exploration and validation, are
published online. This work extends the existing research on MongoDB's
transactional functionality and provides an actionable guide for developers
wish to set up a single-node MongoDB with a custom validation functionality.

Table Stores (EDTS) held in conjunction with the Conference of Object Oriented Programming Languages (COOLOS).

at https://github.com/SpecFreak/MongoDB-Validation.

We translate complex spatial configurations into a simplified, three-dimensional geometric framework that categorizes networks based on their topology. This topology defines the assembly's symmetry and whether it is unstable or stable. In this context, we examine a specific, intricate network – tri-angulene – with uniquely defined interactions between its components. Each component can exist in one of two possible forms, represented by a circle or a square, and these forms interact differently, with a stronger connection between two components than with the third. This distinction creates an unstable equilibrium between two possible arrangements: a circle surrounded by squares or squares surrounded by circles. If the interaction between components is uneven, the assembly becomes unstable, ultimately leading to a spin-reversal dynamic, where the geometry suddenly and drastically changes. This change is triggered by a minor disturbance and results in a new, stable geometry in the middle of the available spectrum, essentially acting as a shock absorber. In this scenario, the geometry's response to change resembles a triangle-like hysteresis curve, with distinct starting and ending points. However, when the interaction between all components is balanced, the assembly becomes metastable, delaying the spin-reversal dynamic until an external force is applied, where it experiences a sudden and irreversible change, also leading to a shock-like hysteresis response. We also discovered that the assembly's ability to change can be influenced by altering the shape of its components, providing another network dynamics variable. Furthermore, once the balanced state is achieved, the assembly returns to a ground state, essentially memorizing its initial configuration. This research demonstrates how hidden geometric principles can explain the unique behavior of complex networks, specifically tri-angulene nanoassemblies, and how these principles can be used to anticipate and predict the assembly's dynamics in response to varying conditions. This understanding can be applied to other, similar networks, potentially leading to the creation of advanced materials with memory and regulatory capabilities. In the broader context, this discovery highlights the value of geometric theory in explaining physical and chemical phenomena, demonstrating how this theory can be used to anticipate and predict the behavior of complex systems, as well as providing a potential solution for decoding the complex dynamics of other nanoassemblies. A novel phenomenon involving adhesive strips has been investigated, revealing a distinct pattern of cracks that arrange themselves in a particular structure before settling into a random pattern typical of adhesive failure. This initial phase, absent in standard adhesive failure models, progresses into the well-known phase of random crack formation, culminating in the release of the strip. High-speed cameras captured images at thousands of frames per second, revealing the intricate arrangement of cracks in one dimension, and in some cases, two dimensions, with patterns mirroring those seen in random lattice formations. The short time frame of this initial phase poses a challenge for experimental design, but it has been successfully captured using a new method based on time-weighted images. The arrangement of cracks is stabilized by increasing the speed of shedding, but it also leads to a shift in the range of conditions required for its formation. The advent of this arranged phase can be anticipated by monitoring the speed of shedding, and it has a distinctive auditory effect, described as a sharp crackling sound that gives way to a louder rattling noise. The phenomenon of an arranged phase of cracks has implications for our understanding of auditory feedback during adhesive failure, and it has been validated using microphones that captured the sounds of shedding at the same rate of adhesive failure. The complex arrangement of cracks also requires a novel theoretical explanation, involving the interaction of stress and release of energy during adhesive failure, and it has been achieved using a new model based on time-dependent lattice gas auto-organization, offering a framework for further investigation into this phenomenon. The unique patterns of cracks and their relationship with auditory feedback during shedding make this phenomenon intriguing, and it has been consistently reproduced in multiple trials, awaiting further analysis and experimentation. The potential applications of this research lie in the fields of adhesion andauditory feedback, with the arranged phase of cracks providing a challenging problem for theoretical validation, and the time frame of its occurrence offering possibilities for real-time experimental design. Social mobility across generations is a long-standing and complex issue, and its dynamics are influenced by various factors including economic opportunities, family background, and the effectiveness of public policies. This paper explores the distribution of future social mobility prospects among different socioeconomic groups by creating a mathematical model that considers the interaction between these factors and the impact of policy interventions. Our analysis shows that the distribution of future social mobility prospects can be influenced by changing factors over time, and that public policies that aim to improve equality through targeted benefits may sometimes exacerbate inequality, rather than reducing it. This paradoxical effect occurs because such policies can benefit higher-income individuals more, due to their greater access to resources and better educational options. This, in turn, leads to a more significant concentration of prospects among the wealthy. Conversely, policies that benefit lower-income individuals more equally could lead to more equitable social mobility. This finding is consistent across various mathematical models, including those that incorporate uncertainty and historical data on demographic trends. This research highlights the importance of careful consideration and accurate analysis in designing effective public policies that aim to improve social mobility and reduce inequality. It also emphasizes the need for a more dynamic perspective when studying the distribution of social mobility prospects among different socioeconomic groups. This paper's results can be applied to a wide range of contexts, from the distribution of prospects in a small community to the global distribution of social mobility prospects among different socioeconomic groups. This is especially relevant for policymakers, economists, and academics who study the intricate relationship between social mobility, inequality, and the effectiveness of public policies in dynamic environments. This finding can be interpreted through various theoretical lenses, including the idea that the distribution of prospects is influenced by the interplay between the factors that determine social mobility, and that it can be affected by changing factors over time, as well as the concept of the "Matthew Effect," which describes how those who are more successful tend to become more successful still. This paper describes the method used to analyze the beam size of the x-ray beam at the ID-29 beamline at ESRF. To precisely determine the vertical size of the x-ray beam, we utilized a scan of the x-ray beam's intensity across its horizontal axis, relying on the assumption that the beam's shape is uniformly distributed and Gaussian in both dimensions. Our analysis of these data sets allowed us to model the signal as a product of two Gaussian functions, one associated with the horizontal dimension and the other with the vertical dimension, using a non-linear method to extract the parameters of these Gaussian functions. Ultimately, our analysis resulted in a precise determination of the beam's vertical size, with an estimated uncertainty of around 1%. Our research also highlighted the importance of properly accounting for detector non-linearity when analyzing scan data, particularly in the context of brightness measurements. The study into Forsage can be useful for conducting similar analyses of other similar scams, as well as providing a framework for identifying and disrupting these operations. We investigate key properties of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the non-ordinary (distributional) Fourier development of functions within these spaces. A key finding shows that the ordinary Fourier expansion of a function defined by a specific operator does not necessarily imply that the function itself is smooth and thus belongs to a specific Gelfand-Shilov space. Additionally, under certain growth restrictions, we establish the relationship between Banach spaces composed of smooth functions under their Fourier descriptions and show that these spaces are equivalent to spaces defined by the norm of the highest order derivative. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the classes of Beurling, Bloch, and Siegel domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$ and hyperbolic domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$, providing a unified framework for understanding these domains and the associated operator systems, including the Bergman space, the polyharmonic system, the $C^k$ system, the strongly elliptic system, the hypoelliptic system, and the Malgrange-Leray system. Lastly, we provide a comprehensive discussion on the composition of the operator with functions from these domains and the associated stability results, as well as a key theorem on the continuous dependence of the solution on the parameter. We conclude by examining a specific model, a Schr\"odinger equation with a time-dependent potential, and analyzing the non-ordinary Fourier development of the solution and its derivative, as well as the operator system that arises from this analysis and its connection to the Gelfand-Shilov space $S^1(\mathbb{R})$. This discussion is accompanied by a comprehensive bibliography of referenced works.

Type II giants and supergiants experience photospheric fluctuations in temperature and luminosity due to oscillations in the inner layers of the star, which can occasionally result in massive ejections of gas and material.  A powered explosion on the stellar surface, rather than seismic waves, is suspected for the massive gas ejections observed in some of these stars.  Our current state of knowledge about these events lacks a clear picture, primarily due to the limited observational data available to us.  The vast amount of optical data for the massive eruption event of AD Leo in 1985 is exceptional, with comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic information that allows us to thoroughly examine this event in the near-ultraviolet spectrum, a range that was partially recorded by the spacecraft IUE.  Our contemporary model of the stellar atmosphere, combined with the data from IUE and other sources, enables us to investigate the massive eruption of AD Leo in the near-ultraviolet range, a range that is critical to understanding these events, and to test various explosion models on the stellar surface, and the importance of mass loss as a possible cause of the eruption.  Our analysis of the data and various models suggests that the massive eruption of AD Leo was likely caused by the loss of about 0.01 solar masses of gas and material, and was powered by a explosive energy of approximately 2.3 x 10 to the 33rds ergs.  This exceptional event occurred about 10 to the 5th years after the discovery of its associated pulsation, which is a notably long period for this type of event, and may help explain the differences in the masses of the ejected gases and the time frames in which they are released.  This research was originally published in the journal Astrophysical Letters, in the issue Volumes 64, the article number is 161.  This finding about the long period of this event may have implications for our current state of knowledge about the mechanisms that cause the mass ejections of Type II giants and supergiants, and the importance of detecting near-ultraviolet continuum in these events, and the use of IUE-like spacecraft in the current era, with the vast amount of observational data available to us, which is exceptional, with the launch of the MEGAN instrument on the spacecraft UVES. In recent years, Point Cloud models have gained significant traction due to their ability to efficiently capture complex 3D surfaces. Nonetheless, these models face difficulties when it comes to large-scale applications, primarily because of the substantial amount of data they encompass. A prevalent issue with Point Cloud models arises during the rendering process, specifically when they fail to adhere to certain continuity standards, thereby causing visual discomfort. To address this issue, researchers have successfuly employed smoothing techniques, albeit most current methods overlook the significance of transformation-dependent information, which is crucial for achieving more realistic and varied outcomes. In this paper, a novel technique called TPC (Transformation-Dependent Smoothing for Point Cloud Representations) is presented, which incorporates transformation-dependent information derived from 3D objects in a supervised setting, using neural networks. When put through rigorous testing on multiple datasets, TPC demonstrated a notable enhancement in quality and versatility, as reflected in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Moreover, this paper highlights a new evaluation metric called Continuity Factor (CF), as well as a simplified implementation for rendering pipelines. TPC has been successfully applied in various real-world scenarios, including video game development, movie production, and statistical analysis of 3D surfaces. This technique is now openly available on GitHub, awaiting further optimization and enhancements. When applied to general Point Cloud data without specified continuity standards, TPC can be simply reconfigured as S4PC, a general-purpose smoothing model that has also been made publicly available on GitHub. This model has been optimized for use with large-scale datasets and provides a balance between processing speed and output quality, offering multiple settings that can be tailored to suit various application requirements. This model has been successfully integrated into various applications, including 3D printing, geographic mapping, and autonomous transportation, among others. S4PC has been designed to handle a broad spectrum of data, from relatively small datasets to massive Point Cloud data exceeding 10 million points, without sacrificing overall performance. This model can be easily deployed across different platforms, either cloud-based or locally, and is compatible with popular deep learning frameworks, enabling seamless integration into various pipelines and development environments. This model provides numerous settings for optimal results in various applications, enabling users to achieve a balance between processing speed and output quality, primarily through the adjustment of layer frequencies, neural network weights, and sampling ratios, all of which can be tailored to suit various requirements by making use of the available code on GitHub. In this work, we introduce a new method that uses impact information and cluster K-means++ initial points to determine the number of states a dynamical system has, and then performs data-driven modeling to obtain mathematical models for these states. We demonstrate how this approach can be part of an effective strategy to handle hyperparameter uncertainties in the context of state estimation and model learning. Specifically, we determine the number of states and initial points, then apply the algorithm responsible for determining the number of states multiple times to obtain a reliable estimate, and finally use this result to inform a grid search for the best model among various candidates. We apply this method to three distinct systems featuring nonlinear dynamics, and show that it yields consistent results in comparison to other evaluation metrics. In addition, we find that in cases where there is uncertainty in the number of states, a method that requires this information, such as grid search, may not significantly outperform our proposed algorithm, which requires the introduction of additional hyperparameters, such as the size of the search grid, but has the advantage of determining this number automatically. Our results are applicable to systems where there is little to no knowledge available about the underlying dynamics, and in such scenarios we show that our method can be effectively combined with data-driven learning methods, such as neural networks, to obtain accurate predictions and model learning. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/AMDoostmohtadi/Data_Guided_Clustering.

In recent years, adversarial text generation techniques have greatly improved, enabling the automatic creation of vast amounts of high-quality data. A significant challenge in this process is allocating an optimal amount of computational resources for opponent modeling, given the limited time available for pre-training. To address this issue, we introduce SparseGAN, a novel adaptive opponent learning algorithm for efficient text generation. By dynamically determining the level of opponent model sparseness in response to changing conditions, SparseGAN's architecture allows for optimized performance and efficient resource allocation across different pre-training and training phases. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that SparseGAN's adaptive opponent learning leads to consistent performance gains, with a 25% improvement in F1 score on sensitive groups and significant reductions in parameter sizes during ongoing training. Furthermore, our findings are reinforced by the analysis of a user interactively fine-tuning a large language model using SparseGAN. The code for SparseGAN is publicly available at https://github.com/Paradox-THU/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another via panspermia, potentially originating from interstellar space, is both captivating and complex. While this concept has been theoretically plausible for a long time, it's also been subject to skepticism due to the harsh conditions it would need to survive, including extreme sunlight, cosmic rays and extreme temperatures. To better understand the feasibility of detecting life transported in this manner, we need to determine how viable it would be for microbial life to thrive in interstellar dust particles during their long journey through the cosmos. In our study, we examined the variety of conditions that astrophysical dust particles could encounter as they travel through the universe and explored the likelihood of microbial life surviving within these particles. We also investigated the possible methods that could be used to identify such life forms, focusing on the utility of spectroscopic analysis and the potential for direct detection of particles harboring life. Our research supports the idea that it's feasible with current technology to recognize life inhabiting interstellar dust particles, although it's essential to note that any successful detection efforts would need to account for the diverse conditions these particles could encounter and the varied timescales over which they spend time in the interstellar medium. We propose a theoretical framework for identifying life in this context and provide a specific example of how this could be achieved by detecting the signs of oxygen released by photosynthetic life forms on dust particles located in the vicinity of nearby cool white dwarf stars. Our study also highlights the potential for the life transported in this manner to influence the composition of exoplanetary atmospheres and the surrounding interstellar medium, leading to observable effects on the surrounding gas and dust. Consequently, we suggest that future surveys focused on detecting the signs of life in exoplanetary atmospheres should also incorporate the possibility of life transported via panspermia and consider the potential for life to be present in the form of dust particles located within a light year of the Earth. Our research emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive approach that takes into account all the possible pathways by which life could be identified on exoplanets, including the possibility of it being transported there via interstellar dust particles. We conclude by outlining the promising outcomes of our analysis and proposing areas for which future investigations are necessary to advance our understanding of this complex and captivating topic. A new model has been developed which incorporates capture location data and choice of trap locations to estimate home range and resource choice models simultaneously.  By removing the need for camera location data to be supplied externally, this model enhances the analysis of capture-recapture data in controlled trap locations. In this research, we focus on the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks composed of nonlinear oscillators, and explore the effects of different connection patterns between the layers on the transmission of signals. With an aim to maintain the simplicity and clarity of our findings, we restrict our analysis to a single-layer network composed of identical, nonlinear oscillators. By utilizing the method of center manifolds to achieve our asymptotic goals, we establish the existence of a unique solution for the multilayer system, and further demonstrate the convergence of solutions across layers through the application of a relevant metric. Furthermore, we introduce a transmission layer graph that is topologically consistent with the original network, and prove that the impact of the transmission of signals between layers can be disregarded as time tends to infinity. Ultimately, this research is presented as a follow-up to our previous work on the stability of damped multilayer networks, with an added layer of signal transmission between the networks. In this extended version, we include three notable cases of connection patterns between layers, as well as numerical examples that demonstrate our findings through simulation. Numerical simulations of black holes and cosmic expansion rely on the assumption that the Universe is roughly symmetric in all directions. Generating accurate data for radial perturbations alone has proven challenging due to the significant computational power required. A new method generates radial data from angular perturbations in the time-domain, using wavecoupling. This approach accelerates simulations of radial perturbations by 100 times, allowing for the inclusion of radial gravitational waves in simulations of binary black hole mergers with moderate mass ratios. It also enables the stable numerical construction of curved spacetime perturbations necessary for testing the general relativity framework. This method has been successfully integrated into the Einstein Toolkit and applied to simulations of binary black hole mergers and expanding cosmic models. It paves the way for more efficient and realistic simulations of mergers and cosmic expansion in the presence of symmetries. In addition to this, it provides specific perturbed metrics that can be used to test the consistency of numerical simulations of mergers and cosmic expansion. The code for this method is available openly via GitHub. The Nernst effect plays a significant role in the rotation of magnetic fields and is typically opposed by a torque on spin polarization. This aligned response is rare and unique, occurring deep within the ferromagnetic phase, and it cannot be explained by conventional theories. Instead, it is thought to result from a complex interplay between electronic and magnetic interactions that need further investigation. This distinctive Nernst response is resistant to suppression by temperature and remains significant even at relatively high temperatures. It is also resistant to electronic scattering and remains unaffected by the insertion of a heavy metal layer between the Mn$_3$NiN and the measurement interface. This distinctive Nernst response is unique to Mn$_3$NiN and has not been observed in other materials, suggesting it could serve as a distinguishing feature for this material. It is thought that this aligned Nernst response could be a manifestation of a rare phenomenon called the Nernst effect anti-damping, however more research is needed to confirm this hypothesis. It is also possible to enhance this aligned Nernst response by replacing the Ni with other transition metals, which could potentially make this material more intense. We address a class of periodic barrier issues involving second-order differential equations with delay-dependent coefficients. Our main achievement is identifying conditions under which solutions to these problems vary uniformly. Specifically, we establish that when the coefficient $p(t)$ satisfies an integrable condition and the coefficient $q(t)$ meets a subquadratic growth requirement, there are constants $C_1, C_2$ for which the solution $u(\cdot)$ satisfies the estimate $C_1\left(\int_{0}^T |u(t)|^2 dt\right)^{1/2} \leq C_2\left(\int_{0}^T |f(t,u(t),u([0,t]))|^2 dt\right)^{1/2}$ holds true. Our solution contributes to the broader context of established results on the uniformity of solutions to differential equations with delay-dependent coefficients and provides a specific case where the solution's uniformity relies solely on a comparison with the parent equation, without any absolute bounds. Furthermore, we establish that, under certain conditions, solutions to these problems vary continuously. The paper also examines the case where the coefficient $p(t)$ meets a Carathéodory condition, for which we obtain a regularity result involving the solution and its derivative. Additionally, we establish the existence and the uniformity of solutions to a class of nonlinear differential equations with delay-dependent coefficients and vanishing damping. The paper concludes by exploring the case where the coefficient $p(t)$ meets a sublinear growth requirement, for which we obtain a result involving the solution's decay. The paper's findings also relate to a specific class of stochastic differential equations with delay-dependent coefficients and vanishing damping, for which we establish the existence and the ergodicity of solutions. The paper ends by providing an overview of the key results that can be found in the literature and providing an appendix containing the proof of an important lemma. The notion that complex systems can benefit from simple components has become a widely accepted principle, often used to justify the use of linear regression models over more sophisticated alternatives. This paper examines the relationship between component complexity and overall system performance, exploring how the inherent properties of tasks influence the optimal level of component complexity. We illustrate this concept through a series of synthetic experiments and a real-world example involving football teams. Our analysis reveals a more nuanced connection between component complexity and overall performance, one that is influenced by the unique characteristics of each task. We then discuss the implications of these findings for how models are selected and validated, particularly with respect to the use of features versus regression models. By taking a more nuanced view of component complexity and system performance, we hope to contribute a more astute understanding of the intricate connections within complex systems. This research was presented at the 21st International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications held in 2021.

In this paper, we demonstrate how geometric metrics may be applied to tensors represented in multi-dimensional spaces, and provide a workable example to illustrate this concept. Traditional tensor analysis focuses on algebraic methods to investigate nonlinear relationships, yet it can also incorporate geometric approaches to examine these connections. This paper shows that metrics derived from geometric formulas can be used as components in tensor representations, and by doing so, it provides a new perspective on the information presented in tensors. Specifically, we use the specific example of a tensor representation based on the Minkowski metric in a multi-dimensional space to illustrate this concept, and in doing so, we highlight the benefits of this approach, including the accessibility of underlying assumptions and the ease with which simulations can be performed. This approach is applicable to a broad range of scenarios, including nonlinear dynamic systems, and it provides a promising foundation for research and development in various fields, including but not limited to physics, economics, and biology. Additionally, it enables a more precise identification of the parameters that define these systems, and it provides a more efficient means of performing simulations and model validation. This approach also provides a framework for model construction, prediction, and validation, and it allows for the development of multi-layered tensor models, among other possibilities. Topological materials possess unique properties resulting from the interplay of electronic and crystalline structures. By integrating random impurities into these materials, topological Anderson localization can be avoided and topological Anderson conductors may be induced, allowing for the guidance of directed energy flows while maintaining stability. Although theoretical models predicting topological Anderson localization exist, induced conductivity remains an unexplored area in experimentation. This work develops methods for incorporating random digital signals directly into integrated circuits used to study topological materials and demonstrates the potential for digital perturbations to create topological Anderson conductors in 2D topological insulators. Furthermore, we identify potential candidates for such digital perturbations among established semiconductor devices, with an emphasis on their impact on the topological properties as defined by bulk and edge mode behavior in a 2D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Specifically, we find that both coupled and isolated digital elements can serve as topological Anderson conductors in separate scenarios. The integration of random digital signals is visualized, in addition to the effects of continuous analog signals, which demonstrate the resilience of topological properties when transitioning from a 1D to a 2D architecture. The digital realization of these experiments is highly accessible and the theory underlying it can be applied to a broad range of integrated circuit configurations, making this breakthrough a significant step towards fully controlling random impurities in integrated circuits used to study topological materials. The induced conductivity and topological properties in this system are further validated through the calculation of effective mass, topological gap, and edge mode behavior. We explore a decentralized learning model known as distributed situational linear bandits, where agents in different environments make decisions and learn from the results. This research focuses on a variety of settings, from non-contextual linear bandits to contextural linear bandits. We establish general bounds on the cumulative regret and identify specific conditions under which tighter bounds hold. A key finding is that, without additional assumptions, learning at a rate of $\tilde{O}(Kd^2T)$ is possible in general. This achievement comes from a variety of existing results and new approaches. Our work also introduces a new method called Distributed Contextual Feedback Linearization, which is the first to be presented. This approach is effective for contextural linear bandits and yields a bound of $\tilde{O}(d^2T)\binom{\log K}{2}$ on the cumulative regret when there are $K$ environments. In contrast, a much tighter bound of $\tilde{O}(d^2T K)$ would typically hold for the same scenario without consideration of context. This finding highlights the negative impact of context on learning within this model. Despite the challenging setting, our work also enables us to learn from a single sample within each environment, which is a notable achievement. This research is accompanied by an lower bound that facilitates an understanding of the proposed algorithm's performance within the framework of distributed situational linear bandits. Our results were previously presented at the COLT 2021 Conference. The updated version of the paper is now available. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate through deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on the control system development for a jumping monopod moving on soft ground, with particular emphasis on ground state estimation and control. Furthermore, a critical height threshold was established to ensure successful takeoff in a single leap. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, leading to the creation and enhancement of turbulence, and ultimately influencing the development and growth of particles like dust. The VSI impact, however, varies significantly depending on the depth and density of the particles, and requires high computational power to simulate in full detail. This study relies on co-simulation methods, combining dust development models with VSI models, to analyze the VSI impact on particle development. The results show that VSI successfully distributes itself across the depth of the disk system, stimulating particle development more intensely in the middle layers than in the upper and lower layers. Furthermore, VSI develops a unique pattern in the mid-layer region, requiring at least a 0.1 scale height to reach full distribution depth. In addition, a notable finding indicates that VSI's impact on particle development becomes less intense as the particle size increases, potentially influencing the likelihood of particles reaching a particular scale in specific regions of the disk system. These conclusions have implications for observing dust particles in real-world disk systems, and highlight the significance of considering dust development in noise emissions observed at specific wavelengths. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that harmonic functions that are bounded or tend to zero at infinity must be constant. This result extends the applicability of the classical Liouville's theorem and has significant implications for a specific class of parabolic manifolds. Furthermore, it provides a crucial boundary condition for potential applications in a broader framework of manifolds with increasing volume. As an illustration of its utility, we have obtained a first-order estimate for the rate of volume change in a particular type of manifolds where the Ricci curvature decreases and the scalar curvature remains constant, and have established that there are no solutions to a specific Yang-Mills-Higgs equation in this context. Lastly, we have obtained results for an open and closed version of a particular type of manifolds where the Ricci curvature decreases and the scalar curvature remains constant, which have been previously studied by other researchers using alternative methods. The key theorem has been derived from the mean value theorem, and its utility has been demonstrated through its application to specific geometric equations, thereby providing a potential foundation for future research in the field. The research has been conducted in collaboration with Guo Zhengfeng. Recently introduced dynamic entrance structures have been gaining attention and have achieved high performance in various machine learning applications. These techniques enable selective data routing by assigning different weights to input streams based on their contents. However, incorporating these models typically follows a linear approach, where streams are combined using weighted summations. In this research, we propose modifying dynamic entrance networks by employing a global mean pooling mechanism across all input streams. This leads to a non-linear, efficient data routing process, where the inclusion of each stream is determined by its overall mean rather than a linear combination of individual elements. We have thoroughly evaluated this novel model and found it to excel in multiple tasks, surpassing the performance of its linear counterpart and existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our model demonstrated superior performance in classification tasks when applied to settings involving multiple classes and in models with multiple attention mechanisms, and also showed significant improvements in various speech processing applications. Moreover, we have provided a comparative analysis of our model's performance in comparison to established methods, in addition to providing code availability online. Our proposed model's efficacy in various contexts makes it an appealing addition to the field of machine learning.

To effectively grasp the underlying semantics of questions, a model like CCSQA, which deals with real-world knowledge, requires a strong understanding of question semantics, especially when faced with ambiguous or partially inaccurate information. To enhance a model's ability to accurately explore question semantics, we propose a two-phase framework known as Semantic Connect (SemCon), initially employing a coarse search to identify a model that provides a preliminary understanding of the desired information, and then conducting a more rigorous verification to validate the accuracy of the desired information. To further analyze the semantic connections between questions and possible answers, SemCon also assesses relationship features associated with the intended meaning of the question. We have tested this approach on a range of open-domain CCSQA tasks and found it to be highly effective in uncovering the underlying semantics of questions and providing more precise answers in complex real-world scenarios. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghru/SemCon.

Quantum chaos in infinite systems can manifest as highly interlinked and complex dynamics, affecting how atoms in an orbiting black hole regime interact with each other and local matter. To study these intricate connections, our novel graph neural network-based analysis, coupled with a hybrid relativity tool, uncovers the localized areas where atoms' waves overlap and demonstrate highly erratic behavior, even in the presence of symmetric conditions. By utilizing a simple metric to measure this erratic behavior, we are able to visualize the uneven distribution of chaotic connections across the system. Our research showcases that the geometry of a black hole's accretion disk holds significant structural information when analyzed through the lens of quantum chaos, a concept first introduced by William H. Misner. Our findings are relevant to the study of high-energy physics and provide a tangible understanding of a complex theoretical idea. Our code is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/Quantum-Relativity/Graph-Neural-Networks-in-Relativity}.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) addresses the challenge of modeling an individual's knowledge structure based on their interactive history with a computerized adaptive system. Despite the widespread use of Deep Learning techniques in KT tasks, there's a lack of standardized evaluation protocols. This issue persists due to varied data collections methods, multiple possible KT system architectures, and differing performance metrics used across studies. As a result, it becomes difficult to compare and contrast these systems and their underlying techniques. This paper presents PyKT, a Python-based evaluation framework designed to facilitate a standardized evaluation process for Knowledge Tracing systems. PyKT introduces an uniform data representation format called Knowledge Tracing Data Object (KTDO), along with a set of recommended evaluation practices for KT system developers. By utilizing this framework, researchers can easily share KTDO-formatted data and reproducibly evaluate various Knowledge Tracing systems. Overwhelming community response to the initial PyKT publication has resulted in the creation of three additional features: multi-thread capable data loaders for increased efficiency, enhanced visualization tools for easier interpretation of results, and a flexible API for easy integration with preferred deep learning frameworks. These additions further enhance PyKT's capabilities and provide a comprehensive platform for standardized Knowledge Tracing system evaluation. The updated framework along with example data and system codes are available online at https://mmlab.github.io/PyKT/.

Creating a standardized proof format across different Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers enables advanced techniques for handling errors and validating the accuracy of solvers. This talk introduces Alethe, a Python library that provides a versatile framework for both publishing and verifying SMT proofs, and it serves as a foundation for discussing the benefits and challenges of a unified proof standard, as well as possible pathways to implementing it. Unlike a static proof format, Alethe enables solvers to generate proofs that are dynamic and executable, effectively turning the process of proving theorem correctness into a problem of theorem proving itself. We will also explore various scenarios, including developing a verifier that can validate the validity of a proof, as well as integrating Alethe with existing solvers and issuing a call for collaboration to advance this project further. This project is part of the NIST's solicitation on Formal Verification Relying Testing, and it is being developed in conjunction with the Yosys SMT flow.

Second, we introduce a new FL algorithm, capable of handling unconstrained gradients, without the need for gradient clipping or other similar constraints. Our findings highlight the difficulties faced by current FL algorithms with constrained gradients, including FL algorithms with clipped gradients, in unconstrained settings, as demonstrated in our experiments. At high pressures, matter is comprised of a multitude of coupled fluids that govern a system's behavior through various equations of state. Despite this, the theoretical framework of these complex systems within the context of General Relativity is often modeled using a single-fluid approach, primarily due to the intractability of multi-fluid Einstein equations. A recent study by Baccetti, Ghilberti, and Lousto developed a method for handling these equations in a semi-analytical manner, thereby facilitating the examination of matter's pressure and density within non-rotating neutron stars. Conversely, their approach revealed that such stars cannot be accurately described using a single-fluid model, as it cannot properly account for the occurrence of phase transitions within those regions nearest to the star's core. On the other hand, this semi-analytical technique can also be applied to static, axially symmetric objects composed of distinct fluids under the influence of gravity, and such objects are often referred to as "barotropic bodies." These bodies are characterized by fluid density profiles that are solely dependent on the distance from the object's center. Within this context, any transition from one fluid to another is confined to specific radial locations, essentially creating a step-function in the form of the density distribution. If such a distribution is matched to the semi-analytical solutions, it becomes possible to determine the precise location of any fluid transition through the analysis of gravitational field equations in a self-gravitating system. In the process, it has been demonstrated that a first-order phase transition, as postulated by the Oppenheimer-Volterra boundary, is a stable equilibrium point that can be confirmed through the application of this semi-analytical method to a specific model involving neutron star matter. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Rectification models rely on large amounts of data for multiple domains. However, achieving domain-specific GER performance often runs into the problem of limited data availability. In response to this challenge, few-shot domain transfer learning becomes an appealing solution. To address this issue, we present a novel approach that leverages the meta-learning framework to transfer GER knowledge across domains with limited data. The resulting model, which we call Meta GER, first undergoes a preliminary training program spanning multiple domains without any constraint on grammar correctness. Subsequent evaluation tasks on a range of domains with different GER standards require correction of errors according to their specific grammatical rules. Our analysis reveals that Meta GER achieves notable improvements over the baseline baseline, demonstrating superior performance in comparison to conventional approaches, and showcasing consistent enhancement over a range of reference standards, including the F score. Furthermore, meta-analysis reveals that the model's capacity to learn underlying GER structures and rules from a few examples enables it to efficiently adapt to novel domains with little data, a finding supported by presentations at the conference. In particular, the data annex includes 14 new domains with available data for training, testing and evaluation, representing 7 language pairs at three different domain levels, namely primary, secondary and tertiary domains. This paper presents a novel approach to codebook design and feedback encoding, leveraging the unique characteristics of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) to enhance performance. Researchers examine the complexities of auxiliary services procurement by vendors in the electricity market.  They identify three prominent issues: pricing mechanisms, supply disruptions, and manipulation risks.  To address these challenges, a mathematical model has been developed which maximizes vendor profits while ensuring fair prices and reliable grid operation.  However, manipulating the system for personal gain remains a possibility.  To prevent this, a one percent penalty is introduced for vendors who engage in price manipulation.  The model's effectiveness was tested on a small sample of data from the Australian electricity market with promising results.  Compared to existing methods, the new model reduces the risk of price manipulation and supply disruption by up to 90% in the tested scenario.  This research provides a framework for policymakers, operational managers, and vendors which enables them to make informed decisions about auxiliary services and market design.  The model can be applied to similar problems in other industries and has implications for theoretical studies of research on the Australian electricity market. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by massive seasonal variations, driven by the planet's axial tilt. As cloud-streak patterns in the northern hemisphere move from winter to summer, they transform from a strong vortex at the pole's center and flowing storm patterns farther away from it. Until now, it has been difficult to pinpoint the exact time of their formation, missing important insights into the dynamics and processes involved. In 2020, a distinctive hexagonal shape approximately 4,500 kilometers in width and centered at 75 degrees north latitude became visible, preceding the equinox and providing a rare opportunity to study the formation of the northern polar vortex in the northern hemisphere's summer. This report details the observations of this unique hexagon and surrounding cloud-streak patterns, featuring the emerging north polar vortex and the decreasing temperature at the pole's core. It also delves into the possible reasons for the sudden appearance of the hexagon and the associated variations in cloud-streak patterns, ultimately leading to the vortex's formation and the tightening of its core. The appearance of the hexagon and the associated variations in cloud-streak patterns and temperature are thought to be caused by the increasing amount of sunlight and the resulting warming of the polar atmosphere, but more research is needed to confirm this hypothesis. This report's findings are based on high-resolution images obtained by the Cassini spacecraft in 2020 and 2021, utilizing a combination of true color and near-infrared photography. It provides a detailed analysis of the hexagon and surrounding cloud-streak patterns, featuring the developing north polar vortex and the decreasing temperature at the pole's core. This study's data and insights are now being used to validate a global circulation model of Saturn's atmosphere, offering valuable knowledge about the dynamics of the planet's polar atmosphere and the processes that shape its cloud-streak patterns and seasonal variations. This report's findings have important implications for understanding the dynamics of the polar atmosphere on other gas giants, particularly Jupiter and Neptune, and providing a deeper insight into the complex processes that govern their cloud-streak patterns and seasonal variations. This research can be extended further by studying the changing patterns of cloud-streak patterns and the associated variations in temperature and the developing summer polar vortex in the northern hemisphere of Saturn, and comparing it with the contrasting winter patterns in the southern hemisphere. This report's findings can also be used as a basis for a future study on the formation of the southern polar vortex in the southern hemisphere of Saturn during its summer, providing a rare and in-depth analysis of the processes that shape the polar atmosphere

In written communication between humans and AI, certain discourse markers such as "thanks" or "sorry" hold significant value, revealing essential aspects about the interaction including the intent behind it and the level of satisfaction derived from it. Unfortunately, without a suitable tool to analyze these markers, researchers are currently limited to reviewing conversations on a marker by marker basis, making it extremely difficult to extract broad insights from a conversation. This paper presents DiscSense, a cutting edge tool that employs artificial intelligence to automatically mine discourse indicators from conversations, thereby enabling researchers to gain a deeper understanding of interactions with AI via discourse analysis. This tool can be applied to a variety of conversations and incorporates an interactive dashboard in its dashboard functionality, equipping developers with a means to extend its discourse indicator detection capability. We highlight DiscSense's capabilities by applying it to a dataset of conversations with a particular intent, further illustrating the tool's efficacy in uncovering intent-related discourse indicators and providing a precise intention prediction accuracy of 90% in addition to generating an interactive dashboard that showcases the diversity of discourse indicators associated with that intent. We believe that DiscSense's capabilities can be expanded to enhance existing dialogue systems and rich text based interaction systems involving AI. The code for DiscSense is available at https://github.com/AI-Research/DiscSense. We present DiscSense at the occasion of submitting it to the conference. We demonstrate DiscSense's versatility in analyzing conversations involving multiple intents by incorporating the Amazon Alexa as an example in the appendix of this paper. We investigate matrix decomposition problems under a fixed-rank constraint, which can be viewed as an extension of classical matrix optimization problems. Utilizing the Riemannian matrix manifold framework, we reformat these problems as first-order or second-order optimizations on matrix manifolds. The fixed-rank matrix decomposition problem involves a nonconvex version, a convex version with rank-limited matrices, and an orthogonally-constrained version. We explore the landscape of these problems, analyzing the presence of local minima, saddle points, and the tightness of the $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ gap in the convex version. Additionally, we establish an initialized geometric convex contraction rate for the nonconvex version and a smooth transition from a highly nonconvex landscape to a geodesically convex landscape as the Riemannian trust-region radius increases. The world-wide landscape analysis is a result of an initiated geodesic $\epsilon$-neighborhood analysis, which may be of independent interest. Furthermore, we provide a rigorous proof of the recently proposed geodesic $\epsilon$-strong convexity, along with an estimated bounding region for the initiated geodesic $\epsilon$-neighborhood. The results presented hold under specific matrix decomposition problems and Riemannian trust-region radius conditions, which are necessary for achieving the desired landscape analysis properties. The paper concludes with an discussion on possible further enhancements and generalizations of the results obtained. The Riemannian matrix manifold framework provides researchers with an versatile tool, offering an in-depth understanding of the complex landscape of fixed-rank matrix optimization problems. We obtained extensive photometric and spectral data for SN 2020jfo, a supernova with a brief plateau characteristic of Type II SNe. Despite its early peak in the I-band within 19.8 days, SN 2020jfo exhibited a typical 100-day luminosity phase. Counter to the typical plateau phase behavior seen in SNe Type II, this event showed a gradual decline in magnitude over two months, returning to a normal Sc II galaxy starlight level. Analyzing the spectral characteristics throughout its development, this supernova initially presented a spectrum akin to 10-20 day SN 1994D, yet later displayed a 60-day SN 1994D spectrum. Co-adding the spectra over narrow frequency ranges, we found that SN 2020jfo initially preferentially absorbed higher frequency light, with its declining phase spectrum more similar to usual Type II SNe. Researchers have long been interested in using the large-scale structure of the universe to predict dark matter halo masses. A key tool for achieving this goal is the cosmic speed field, which represents the flow of galaxies across the universe and is influenced by gravitational attraction towards dense areas and repulsion from sparse regions. The advanced gravitational wave observatories detecting signals from the mergers of neutron stars and black holes present a vast amount of data for researchers to analyze. Combining these observations with electromagnetic radiation will allow a more comprehensive understanding of the universe. However, the electromagnetic detection of such events is rare and often delayed, making it challenging to associate electromagnetic emissions with specific gravitational wave signals. To enhance the efficiency of these associations, developing an efficient method to classify gravitational wave signals is crucial. Our research involves utilizing a neural network based approach to classify injections of simulated gravitational wave signals resulting from neutron star-binary mergers, neutron star-black hole mergers, and black hole-binary mergers based on their waveform characteristics. We tested this network on simulated signals with SNR varying from 8 to 20 and found that it accurately identifies the mass ratios and types with an overall accuracy of 90%. We also explored the minimal number of waveform features required for classification and found that a neural network can effectively classify signals using just 10-20 waveform parameters. Furthermore, we analyzed the sensitivity of our results to different network architectures and found that a simple neural network performs optimally. Our results have implications for future gravitational wave observatories and suggest that neural network based approaches can efficiently classify signals on large datasets. We also discuss the challenges of associating electromagnetic emissions with gravitational wave signals and the importance of developing such neural network based tools for current and future observatories. While dense cores are found in composites and young massive stars, with masses similar to those of their surrounding environments, there is a discrepancy in the mass ratios compared to low-mass stars.  Two possible formation pathways for massive stars have been proposed: accretion of high densities over extended periods, or the merger with high-density stars.  A study of the Beccari et al. database finds that massive young stars typically go through a stage of 10^3 years with free-fall accretion, followed by a decline in mass accretion rates.  Using this information and a simple model, researchers re-examined the core masses of stars in the Beccari et al. database and found that, like cohesive stars, composite stars also lie on a mass ratio line, with ratios similar to those of low-mass stars, formed over 10^3 years with free-fall accretion, with core masses still dependent on the mass of the surrounding environment.  This indicates that massive stars often form through the merger of low-mass stars rather just dense cores, and a model of star-formation that includes both accretion and mergers is supported, with implications for theoretical models of massive star-formation. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring minute variations in local magnetic fields, especially in areas with significant electromagnetic noise. By optimizing the dimensions of the nanowire, we can significantly improve the sensitivity to magnetic field fluctuations, achieving a detection limit of one hundredth of a nanotesla for a single measurement, which could be further enhanced to as low as nanoteslas with additional technical improvements. This level of sensitivity, combined with the ability to scan the location of changes with atomic interferometry, enables the tracing of magnetic field paths with extraordinary precision, and may also facilitate the detection of changes in the gravitational acceleration or the curvature of space-time. A key finding demonstrates that this characterisation aligns with measures that are locally constant and discrete, resulting in the definition of a polynomial algebra $A_n$ that comprises polynomials that reflect the geometric structure of data clusters. Furthermore, the investigation reveals that the space of functions $F_n$ that are derived from $A_n$ contains subfunctions $f_\theta$ that represent the density of each cluster defined by parameters $\theta$, thereby enabling the recovery of original data clusters from the original data distribution. A novel algorithm is also presented that employs a gradient flow to efficiently recover the underlying structure of data clusters. A distinguishing feature of this approach is that it differentiates clusters based on their intrinsic characteristics rather than relying on prespecified metrics such as Gaussian distributions. A real-world application to image segmentation on a large dataset demonstrates both the scalability and effectiveness of this method. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's stability is also provided, along with an expression for the growth of $F_n$ that is applicable to arbitrary datasets. A notable finding of this research is that $F_n$ can be compressed into a compact space $S_n$ that is characterized as the set of subfunctions $f_\theta$ that are defined by unique points $\theta$ in a space defined by the data, resulting in the possibility of recovering original data clusters from a significantly smaller and simplified representation of the original data distribution. This discovery of the intrinsic structure of finite mixture models also clarifies the concept of cluster definitions, demonstrating that clusters are not arbitrary divisions of data but rather divisions that are based on the analysis of a polynomial algebra $A_n$ and result in the recovery of data points that are associated with distinct and discrete measures $\mu_i$ in the space of functions $F_n$. This research on finite mixture models also illustrates the connection between stochastic geometry and Choquet theory, demonstrating how the characterisation of finite mixture models as the mean of measures that represent the distribution of data points with respect to their underlying clusters, using a measure $\mu_i$ to represent the distribution of the $i$th cluster, can be reframed as a problem of defining clusters as the level sets of a subfunction $f$ that is associated with a measure $\mu$ in the space $M_n$.

High-performance computing on GPUs for object-based programming necessitates an advanced memory management system, including dynamic memory allocation and deallocation. Presently, using global memory on GPUs is straightforward and doesn't require explicit memory management; however, this leads to subpar performance and limited scalability. We introduced earlier [1] a memory allocator called SOAr that addresses this challenge by utilizing a combination of global and shared memory on GPUs. Building upon this work, we present DynaSOAr, a state-of-the-art, multi-threaded memory allocator that outperforms the original version significantly. DynaSOAr boasts enhanced performance, a lower hardware failure rate, and reduced memory usage. We also introduced a novel approach called "allocation routing" that accelerates memory allocation and a "fragmentation prevention" technique to enhance memory utilization and minimize memory fragmentation. Additionally, we optimized memory access and reduced data duplication. DynaSOAr was optimized for NVIDIA GPUs, specifically the Ampere architecture. We present comprehensive benchmark results, comparing our allocator to the acclaimed PMR allocator, showcasing DynaSOAr's superiority in various scenarios. Furthermore, we provided detailed implementation guidelines for developers to utilize DynaSOAr efficiently. We demonstrated that DynaSOAr's advanced features come with a minimal performance cost, averaging a 1.25x performance increase over the basic SOAr version. Consequently, we believe DynaSOAr is the most advanced, high-performance memory allocator for object-based programming on NVIDIA GPUs. Experimental results indicate that DynaSOAr delivers outstanding performance in various applications, including deep learning, with a 1.19x performance boost compared to the baseline, against formidable competitors like PyTorch and TensorFlow. Moreover, we found DynaSOAr's performanceadvantages to be evident across different NVIDIA GPU architectures, including the Ampere, Kepler, and Maxwell. We discovered that DynaSOAr's performance to be particularly superior in applications that utilize large memory blocks extensively, such as ResNet-50. We concluded that DynaSOAr's innovative allocation routing and fragmentation prevention techniques, along with its highly optimized memory access and minimal data duplication, all contribute to its remarkable performance. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model, applicable to all impurity states, incorporates magnetic moment influence on the scattering of electrons and incorporates initial principles of electron spin symmetry. It has been successfully integrated with a full-scale first-principles calculation method to predict the spectra of individual manganese atoms and dimers on a niobium surface, and compares favorably with experimental results. This theoretical framework highlights the intersection of quantum mechanics and spin physics in this complex system, and demonstrates how magnetic moment affects electron scattering and influence on the surrounding electron sea. It also provides a precise explanation for a previously unexplained spectral feature, and predicts the occurrence of a T-dependent state splitting in the dimer case. This theoretical model can be applied to other magnetic impurities located on superconducting surfaces. If numerical limitations could be overcome, it is anticipated that this model could be integrated with advanced renormalization group methods to better understand remote magnetic influence on the low-energy spectra. This theoretical research was conducted in partnership with experimental researchers who provided accurate magnetic moment values for individual manganese atoms and dimers on a niobium surface, based on scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy results. This collaboration facilitated the prediction of new effects in this system, such as the occurrence of a Kondo collapse in the dimer case, which could be directly observed in experiments. Our study of titanium dioxide doped with carbon and nitrogen uses density functional theory to examine the electronic and magnetic arrangements of isolated defects and their interaction in TiO$_{2}$ solids. We investigated all possible magnetic configurations of these defects, and our results show that in solid form, the orientation of the spin magnetic field can become arranged in various patterns - both disordered or ordered - due to interactions between defects. We found that in solid form, the degree of spin disorder or order can be over a wide range, from a highly ordered state similar to that found in pure titanium dioxide, to a completely disordered state. This variability could contribute to the diversity of ordered or disordered arrangements observed in experimental scans. We also found that in solid form, the distance between oxygen ions near defects can change slightly compared to pure titanium dioxide, which may explain the difficulty in accurately determining the u-gaps of solid films in experiments. We further examined layered rutile titanium dioxide doted with nitrogen and carbon, and found that in solid form, the arrangement of magnetic fields and the distance between oxygen ions can change more significantly - which may result in the formation of defects that behave as electrons rather than holes. We also found that in layered rutile titanium dioxide doted with nitrogen and carbon, the presence of oxygen ions between layered layers may not always be necessary, which may result in formations that behave as metal oxynitrides rather than nitrooxides. We believe that our findings may contribute to the understanding of diverse arrangements observed in experiments, and may also provide guidance on how to theoretically model such diversity using density functional theory. We also made calculations of the energy levels of isolated defects and the u-gaps of solid films, which may be verified in future experiments. We examined two types of N doped arrangements, and found that the energy levels of isolated defects and the u-gaps of solid films can change significantly depending on magnetic arrangements, which may result in the formation of openings rather than electron defects in some N doted arrangements. However, this process has a smaller cross-section than inelastic top-pair production, and its measurement is challenged by the extensive background from similar processes, such as inelastic top-pair production and heavy-quark production combined with missing transverse energy. We propose an alternative analytical method to identify these processes based on the total transverse energy of the collisions, which can be done using the "elastic potential" $E_{\text{ep}}$, defined as the transverse energy of the collisions divided by the transverse momentum of the top quarks. This approach demonstrates that the cross-section of the inelastic top-pair process is significantly reduced at higher $E_{\text{ep}}$ values, indicating that this process primarily produces small transverse energy in the collisions. Furthermore, we show that the cross-section of heavy-quark pair production that is accompanied by missing transverse energy exhibits an $E_{\text{ep}}$-dependent decline, which can be described by a $e$-folding length of approximately 5.7 in the large $E_{\text{ep}}$ regime. In 1993, Erdos, Spinka, and Galvin established a fundamental result in Ramsey theory for infinite graphs, demonstrating that in any coloring of an infinite graph from a two-color palette, at least one monochromatic infinite component exists. Subsequent to this discovery, researchers began exploring variants of this phenomenon, leading to the study of a specific density measure, known as Ramsey upper/density or Ramsey top density, which is sensitive to the size distribution of a graph's infinite components. Here, we develop a initial set of characteristics for this Ramsey top density property, demonstrating its connection to various graphical properties such as infinite subgraphs, locally finite subgraphs, and branches in a tree-like structure. Furthermore, we establish lower bounds on the Ramsey top density of specific graph types, including locally finite subgraphs with a ramsey property, trees, and certain types of bipartite graphs. These results extend and refine existing lower bounds on the Ramsey top density, offering a unified and generalised proof of these results. The development of these results also involves a discussion of its connection to the original Erdos-Gallai tree inequality, leading to a possible extension of this inequality to multi Ramsey settings. The study presented here is accompanied by a companion paper that addresses the multi Ramsey setting. The paper presented here is also a direct extension of a result that originally belonged to the collection of unsolved problems in Ramsey theory. Research indicates that ultra-intense laser interactions with thin material layers may generate highly polarized positron beams containing thousands of particles. To explore the possibility of producing larger positron beams, we investigated laser-interaction effects with thicker targets in this paper. Using comprehensive numerical tools and incorporating relativistically self-consistent electrodynamics, we studied positron production in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. Our findings show that thick targets stocked with high-density matter, capable of reaching a critical point known as a "quantum electrodynamics (QED) saturation point," emit positrons that are significantly polarized, with degrees of polarization reaching 0.5 or more. Furthermore, our study reveals that thick targets modify the positron spectrum compared to thin targets, with positrons produced in the center-forward region being more polarized due to the unique characteristics of the intense electromagnetic fields created in this region. We also discovered that thick targets permit the utilization of higher-energy lasers, leading to enhanced positron polarization in certain situations. Overall, our research indicates that positron polarization is an inherent property of laser-plasma interactions with dense matter and that degrees of polarization as high as 90% are achievable with optimized conditions. Hence, we believe that thick-target experiments offer a promising approach for developing sources of highly polarized high-energy positrons. The most promising scenario analyzed here involves a 5-dj Hou laser interacting with a 5-micron gold foil, with the potential to generate over 10 million polarized positrons per steradian. The polarization degree of these positrons reaches 90% within a 20-degree angular range centered on the axis perpendicular to the laser polarization. The emitted spectrum in this scenario extends up to 20 GeV, with the average energy per particle reaching 6 GeV within the mentioned angular range. The optimized thick-target scenario also exhibits positivity coherence lengths of approximately 10 microns, indicating that positivity remains valid even in the intense field regime created by high-power lasers interacting with dense matter. Consequently, this research validates the use of dense matter targets in experiments involving the study of high-energy physics with ultra-intense lasers, and it opens the door to exploring novel phenomena induced by the interplay between intense light and matter. The findings presented here have been tested using two separate numerical tools, with the results matching exactly. Notably, the majority of these unresolved sources, with masses less than 30 times that of the Sun, are young protostars, while more massive ones, above 30 times that of the Sun, are associated with massive star formation. A study of a prominent dark nebula, containing both dark and infrared bright filaments, provides further insight into this phenomenon. Although it takes about 30 million years for these filaments to evolve from infrared dark to bright, this brief period is sufficient for a significant influence on the surrounding environment, with the dispersed material contributing to massive star formation. A comparative analysis with a model of a turbulent molecular cloud supports this conclusion, revealing that the majority of infrared bright filaments are likely compact by nature, and exhibiting similar dimensions to those of infrared dark filaments, with both types sharing a similar length range, although with distinct density patterns.
