Complex liquid mixtures often encounter resistance from surface tension, pinning points, and rough surfaces, which can vary significantly in intensity and source. While surface curvature and pinning points are well understood, the impact of surface roughness on the flow of fluids has not been universally defined and can be expressed in different ways, such as the Rosseland, Wenzel, and Cassie-Baxter models. In this study, we examine the interaction between surface roughness and the resistance a liquid foam must overcome to flow. By incorporating the effects of surface curvature and different pinning scenarios, we developed an expression for resistance that applies to all levels of surface curvature and pinning intensities, and demonstrated that it can be a very strong influence on a system. In fact, even a small amount of surface curvature or low-level pinning can make a significant difference. To support this finding, we presented specific numerical examples of how resistance changes under various conditions, and also analyzed an earlier experiment on flowing liquid foams. Ultimately, our research provides a general framework for studying the resistance a foam must overcome to flow, and it can be applied to other complex liquids that contain diverse components, and to situations where the degree of surface curvature and component integration may change over time. Furthermore, we found that a much higher level of roughness resistance must be overcome before the normal process of foam drainage is impeded, which has important implications for a variety of biological and environmental processes that involve the breakdown of surface fluids. Lastly, our work on the dynamics of foam flowing through a narrow channel highlights the importance of proper modeling of surface curvature and the integration of components, and it demonstrates how a simple yet effective model can be used to understand and analyze this complex process. This model can be applied to similar situations involving the dynamics of other complex liquids. Lastly, we examined a situation that approximates the Cassie-Baxter state, where a fluid flows over a very rough surface, and found that the degradation of this state, which typically results in the transition to the Wenzel state, can be a very slow process that is influenced by the time it takes for the components of the system to change, rather than any immediate change in surface curvature. This is consistent with the observation that the process of drainage that leads to the Wenzel state is often accelerated by changes in surface curvature. This knowledge can be applied to a wide range of phenomena that involve the flow of fluids on surfaces, and it has significant implications for many biological and environmental processes that rely on the interaction between fluids and surfaces.

The number of skin cancer cases is rising globally, necessitating early and accurate diagnoses to increase treatment effectiveness. 73 different types of skin carcinomas have been documented, making it challenging to create a comprehensive detection system.  Deep learning techniques such as CNN and ASCN have shown significant promise in detecting skin carcinomas from images by revealing their internal patterns and improving robustness to image quality variability. However, these methods have limitations in handling unusual samples and may result in incorrect predictions for newly classified carcinomas. To address this issue, this study introduces a feature disorder technique that makes our model more resistant to unusual samples by introducing structural variations in image features.  To further enhance performance, a custom outlier detection method based on density estimation is employed.  Using this approach, we extracted 57 types of skin carcinomas from the original dataset and used 35 for training, 10 for model selection, and 12 for density estimation parameter tuning.  The remaining 25 types were used for testing and validation.  Our results showed significant performance improvements in detecting unusual samples and a 12.5% reduction in accuracy compared to the baseline.  When applied to the remaining 25 types of skin carcinomas for model retraining and validation, our approach resulted in a 5% accuracy increase.  Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/abdi-rahman/Skin-Carcinoma-Detection.  This study used a specially designed dataset consisting of 25 types of skin carcinomas, with 2000 images at 28x28 pixel resolution, and demonstrated the effectiveness of feature disorder techniques in creating resilient models that can generalize to unseen carcinomas.  However, due to limited access to skin carcinoma image datasets, this study's findings cannot be replicated for other derivation methods.  Nonetheless, this research demonstrates the potential of feature disorder techniques in other dermatological image analysis tasks.  Our proposed approach resulted in a 95th percentile outlier density threshold of 0.0008, indicating that samples with densities below this level are considered outliers.  This study also examined the influence of hyperparameter selection on the proposed approach and found that the proposed approach is sensitive to the number of principal components selected during ASCN and the number of layers in the CNN.  To improve performance, we employed a combination of data augmentation and transfer learning in the CNN.  This study further examined the influence of derivation methods on the proposed approach and found that the proposed approach works well with both random and incremental derivation methods. This research reveals a wide range of dynamic interactions between the interface and the wall, including the formation of finger tips with sharp corners, as well as branches that connect to the interface at points with cuspids. Both the still and rotating scenarios have similar stability characteristics. However, when the cell starts rotating, a sudden transition occurs that results in a cusp forming at the point where the interface meets the wall. This process is accompanied by the formation of a small finger-like structure. This research also demonstrates how the appearance of these cuspids can be influenced by increasing the cell's rotation speed or the interface's speed. It is further observed that these cuspids can develop into sharp cornered fingers that continue to grow as the interface moves further into the cell. In neural machine translation, a key challenge is determining which words to focus on when generating the target language, given that the same tokens can serve different purposes, including as fillers in initial output tokens. To address this, we introduce a novel approach, assigning a focus label to each token based on its position, semantic content, or both, which guides the attention mechanism and prioritizes significant content creation. In a creation-driven setting, we prioritize the creation of initial content by labeling the first token as content and the rest as fillers. Our approach outperforms baseline models in various evaluation metrics. When compared to state-of-the-art models including the Turing Award-winning Transformer, our simple yet effective approach achieves substantial improvements of over 1.5 NTXLLF scores in both small and large translation tasks. Our focus on content creation can also be adapted to other neural machine interpretation tasks, such as summarization, by simply incorporating a mask to limit the generated summary to a defined length. Our code is available at github.com/ghru/focus-nmt.

To achieve this, they drew upon the services of a rule-based translation system, customizing it to facilitate their development process. The resulting grid computing application served as the framework's core, upon which the development team built additional features for a working prototype. Although the project's primary focus lay outside translational development, its experience highlighted both the potential of object-oriented specifications and the efficacy of a particular translational method. Consequently, the development of the Grid Framework has been rebranded, and its underlying architecture, now known as the Translational Framework, will serve as the basis for further experimentation in grid computing. The project's source code and artifacts are available for download via the Apache License. The Translational Framework's success has been demonstrated through the successful deployment of a grid computing application, thereby validating the credibility of both object-oriented specifications and the translational development approach. The multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis method is an extension of the singular spectrum analysis model, accounting for multivariate functional time series data. This research develops three variants of the algorithm for conducting singular spectrum analysis across different dimensional domains, including a fully multivariate variation, as well as versions for paired and univariate data. We demonstrate the performance of these methods through simulated data sets and real-world examples, including atmospheric temperature data and paired financial time series. The results show that the algorithm's ability to forecast and detect cointegration is comparable to that of the multivariate vector autoregression model, with the advantage of requiring significantly less computational resources. The implementation of the method in the R software environment is also made available. The paper is co-authored with Y. Y. Teng, the postgraduate student, and Y. H. Hsieh.

This research investigates the long-term implications of fluctuations in a random walk's duration, a related concept to the famous arcsine law governing the walk's occupation times. Unlike occupation times, which are bounded by one and zero, the walk's duration is defined as the time elapsed since the last time it crossed a given threshold, and it can extend indefinitely. Our main finding shows that, regardless of whether the walk is biased or fair, there is a positive probability that the walk's duration will remain local, i.e., it does not exceed some finite time even as time goes to infinity. In other words, there are trajectories in which the walk's duration at some future time can be made arbitrarily large, yet this is not a generic or typical outcome. In contrast, the probability that the walk's duration exceeds any given large time is approximately proportional to that time, and in the unbiased case, the probability that the walk's duration remains local is proportional to the square root of time. Our results extend to related quantities like the time until the walk leaves a given interval or the time until it returns to a given level. Our approach to achieving these results involves a new theorem that enables us to analyze these problems using a different perspective. Our findings also align with those obtained using a different method presented in the paper. Finally, our research yields concrete estimates of the probabilities in question, which can be useful in its own right. Few studies exist that directly address random walk fluctuations in one dimension, and our results are intended to contribute to the understanding of these fluctuations. Our results are further relevant to the broader context of random walk fluctuations in higher dimensions. Our approach is designed to be broadly applicable and can be used to investigate similar problems in other settings. Our results are also finite-time results, which can provide insights useful for the type of stochastic processes known as continuous-time Markov chains. Our results are further motivated by the connection to the broader context of random walk fluctuations in the plane, specifically the Grunberg-Shi result concerning the probability that the walk remains within a given distance from the origin. A detailed investigation of the plasma characteristics was carried out during the helicon phase, focusing on the relationship between input power and plasma parameters. By comparing the experimental results with a mathematical model, a feature of the plasma boundary was revealed, consistent with an earlier observation. Furthermore, the evaluation of the plasma conditions was completed by analyzing the neutral gas depletion near the plasma source, utilizing a newly developed method. The findings from the plasma analysis were validated through the study of neutral gas depletion in three dimensions, yielding a precise match with the experimental data. The helicon phase of the IShTAR plasma generator effectively replicates the plasma conditions of the stellarator, making it a valuable tool for conducting plasma studies relevant to future stellarators. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, pinpointing and labeling specific types of nuclei, particularly for invasive cancer, proves to be a major challenge. To address this issue, a two-stage convolutional neural network is proposed to efficiently locate and label nuclei efficiently. The first stage of the network, tasked with producing an over-segmented map of the input image, employs a dilated convolution to capture the characteristic round shape of nuclei. The second stage, responsible for discriminating between true nuclei and background, uses a low-resolution map derived from the image by applying spatial averaging to guide its predictions. The proposed network was evaluated on datasets containing invasive cancers and demonstrated superior performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency in comparative tests. Furthermore, significant improvements in data-driven extraction and labeling of nuclei were observed. The technology has been made available on GitHub for public use. The challenges of developing fully automated cancer diagnosis systems are complex and multifaceted, depending on factors like data quality, the specific disease in question, and how the system is applied, but technologies like nucleus segmentation can be an important starting point, and with sufficient training, such systems can be highly accurate, as evidenced by the 97% accuracy achieved in this study. The current version of the technology is limited to 2D images, but it has the potential to be developed further, possibly in conjunction with technologies for segmenting entire cells, which could in turn enables automated analysis of cancer diagnosis. The founding organization, the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Technology, is available to provide further information about the technology and potential areas where it can be applied. The technology has also been patented. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue properties by analysing the internal movements of tissues under low-level vibrations. Despite its potential, this method has limitations in pinpointing specific structures or detecting anomalies in close proximity to the surface. A novel approach, Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA), has been developed to address these constraints by introducing a completely synthetic virtual origin throughout the full aperture, enabling precise estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Consequently, this method extends the imaging range of elastography to a quarter of the aperture length, and significantly enhances the accuracy of frequency shift estimation, a crucial component of the technique. A comparative analysis was conducted with the original method and other advanced techniques, demonstrating the superiority of VOSA in both surface-shaped displacement and frequency shift estimation. A notable finding showed that VOSA yields comparable results with the advanced methods in a short aperture, although it has a more stringent requirement of at least three apertures in length to function effectively. A comprehensive evaluation of VOSA was performed using numerical simulations and experimental data, and the resulting images were compared to reference images obtained using mechanical scanning, revealing a high correlation of 0.93 in both cases. While showcasing the practical use of these systems through real-world applications is challenging due to the lack of established methods for evaluating them. In response, we introduce a novel metric, the Rational Pseudocode Metric (RPM), designed to assess the computational efficiency of pseudocodes generated from successful interactive algorithm demonstrations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RPM by applying it to a broad sample of existing interactive algorithm demonstrations, uncovering insights into the pseudocodes' computational performance, as well as the impact of different evaluation approaches. Finally, we outline the scope for future research, including the integration of RPM with existing metrics, the development of a tool to visualize pseudocodes, and the creation of a dataset for interactive algorithm demonstrations. In the framework of high-dimensional data clustering, we develop a one-parameter family of algorithms known as Adaptive Sorting, which applies to both $k$-means clustering and $k$-median clustering. Our algorithms first conduct an preliminary assessment and categorize data points into a range of groups, and then proceed to accurately determine the centers and group assignments for each group through the use of recursive subdivision and sorting. We achieve guaranteed approximate solutions to both problems and also gain an in-depth understanding of the performance characteristics of our algorithms. Additionally, we establish our results within the broader context of the existing literature by comparing them to the optimal solutions obtained via the use of existing algorithms such as the Famous-Cramer bound and the Super-Sharp Littlewood-Offord bound. In particular, we show that our algorithms yield approximate solutions that are within a small factor of the optimal solutions, and also demonstrate the applicability of our algorithms to the challenging task of high-dimensional data visualization. Our results presented herein are novel and our algorithms are believed to be the first of their kind in the field of high-dimensional data clustering. Our findings also highlight the significance of the use of category-based representations in the context of random matrices. In the course of our proofs, we introduce the use of a novel branching random walk, and also the use of a new large deviation principle specifically designed for random matrices, which may be of independent interest to the expert community. Our results presented herein are further validated through the use of rigorous analytical as well as numerical experiments, which also complement our results by providing both theoretical and practical insights into the design of high-dimensional data clustering algorithms. This work introduces a novel framework for stochastic games that incorporates both pursuit-and-evade and capture-or-escape elements, bridging the gap between these two extreme cases. We classify games into different hierarchy levels based on the relative effectiveness of the player's actions, utilizing a precise mathematical definition that leverages the $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium concept. By doing so, we identify specific conditions that fall into existing categories of hierarchical divisions. A key contribution of this research is the development of hierarchical division frameworks that can be applied to a broad range of situations, even incorporating aspects of zero-sum games. Furthermore, we provide a straightforward algorithm to compute hierarchical divisions in a hierarchical division frameworks. A notable result arises in the simplest scenario, where we derive an optimal policy directly, without relying on the algorithm. This research also explores the relationship between hierarchical divisions and the associated value functions, establishing that their difference fulfills a specific stochastic differential equation. Ultimately, this work provides a comprehensive study of hierarchical divisions, offering a versatile and general framework for a wide range of stochastic games. This research focuses on developing an efficient method for detecting vector bosons, specifically W and Z bosons, in high-energy muon collisions. Due to the vast amount of data involved, a fast vector boson estimation approach is crucial for historical muon data. To achieve this, we investigate two main methods of estimation: maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and neural network-based estimation. Our study evaluates the performance of these two techniques using simulated data from both Z and W boson productions at the LHC. We further explore the impact of various factors on vector boson estimation, including the energy range, charge identification, and neural network parameters. Our results show that the neural network-based estimation yields more accurate outcomes than the maximum likelihood estimation, with differences of up to 20% in certain energy ranges. Furthermore, we find that the neural network's performance can be further enhanced by incorporating additional inputs, such as energy ranges and charge identification, which significantly improves the charge misidentification rate to less than 0.5%. Our most precise estimation of neural network output yields an energy resolution of 5.73 GeV for Z bosons and 5.80 GeV for W bosons. Our research also highlights that using a simpler maximum likelihood estimation, we can achieve an acceptable level of precision with significantly reduced computational demands, which is advantageous for massive data sets. Our most precise estimation of neural network output yields an energy resolution of 5.73 GeV for Z bosons and 5.80 GeV for W bosons. Our findings provide a reliable and highly efficient framework for detecting vector bosons in muon collisions and offer a practical solution for the charge identification of forward-going muons in experiments such as the Muon collider or the future upgrades of the LHC. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/VectorBosonEstimation/VBE.

The pace at which environmental conditions and task definitions are changing in modern reinforcement learning settings is very rapid, and systems being developed for these conditions are not adapting quickly enough to stay relevant, and in fact are often seeing a significant decline in performance, a phenomenon we are terming 'cognitive crumble'. In this study, modules were incorporated into reinforcement learning models that could switch between various tasks, and for the model to succeed, these modules had to be combined into a single, combined module with perfect knowledge of all tasks. A unique feature of this research was using reinforcement learning alone to train the models, without any supervision or correction, and by gradually introducing new tasks and altering existing ones, researchers created a setting that mimicked intense change within task environments. The key finding of this study is that reinforcing learning models of this type leads to a stronger, more adaptable module that not only recovers from disruptions but also shows a significant decrease in the rate at which performance declines in response to new tasks and changes to existing ones, and this improvement extends to a visible recovery from the cognitive crumble effect. Furthermore, this research also discovered that the location in which new tasks are added has a significant impact on learning, with the rate of performance decline being the slowest when tasks are added randomly, and that this system is highly effective in eliminating the memory bias seen in reinforcement learning, by completely disregarding past tasks. This theory was then applied to a complex system of multiple, interconnected systems, and surprisingly, it showed a significant improvement in learning, even when there are changes to the connection between these systems, and also revealed that the rate of performance decline can be influenced by the type of connection between them, with random connections resulting in a much slower rate of performance decline. In conclusion, this study and its findings on a complex model of multiple task environments also known as multi-multi-task reinforcement learning presents a novel approach to learning that breaks down memory biases and reduces the rate of performance decline when there are changes to task environments. This paper develops a 3-spheres theorem for non-negative Clifford analytic functions, which can be viewed as a variant of the mean value property that holds for certain types of analysis functions. A significant consequence of this theorem is the confirmation of a key hypothesis underlying Lewis's generalization of the well-known Hopf boundary lemma for harmonic functions. Additionally, this theorem facilitates a significant extension to its own version of the 3-spheres theorem, originally proven by Avakhumovič, Baričaković, and Kolenderovič for harmonic functions. Furthermore, this extension has been rigorously established for a broader class of analysis functions, albeit with a different formulation. Lastly, this paper's results have been applied to establish the uniqueness of positive solutions to certain semi-elliptic boundary value problems from the field of potential theory. Lastly, this paper's results also imply the extension of the 3-spheres theorem to the field of parabolic potential theory. Both of these extensions have been previously unreported in the scientific literature. The key hypothesis mentioned above, which is a hypothesized consequence of the mean value property, has been validated for the broader class of analysis functions. The paper at hand was inspired by a previously published work by H. Leutwald, whose approaches have been extended and expanded upon to include generalised versions of the 3-spheres theorem and the mean value property. The paper at hand also cites the following references: H. Leutwald, ZAMP, 47, 111 (1996). In situations where measurements are affected by a distorted or degraded medium, inverse problems in physics and engineering typically require their recovery. Researchers have shown that applying a forward model to generated synthetic data that includes the unknown medium, positioned as an additional parameter in the problem, can lead to better results in tasks like radar target recognition, sound source localization, and seismic imaging. These methods typically employ a backward sampling approach under the assumption that the forward model accurately represents the physical principles behind the measurements and the generation process. However, when the forward model is flawed or unclear, our novel proposed framework, a regularized conditional GAN, can be used to overcome this limitation by focusing on the mapping from the measurements to the medium, without the need to specify the forward model explicitly. By using a simple and interpretable objective function that directly incorporates the backward sampling criterion, we established the convergence properties of this algorithm, demonstrating its connection to a regularized conditional GAN. Our experiments on synthetic data and real-world examples, including seismic inversion and radar target recognition, show that this framework can recover the underlying structure of the data and outperforms baseline methods. Our proposed algorithm can be used as a starting point to guide other Bayesian or optimization-based approaches for these applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/AKX2/RCGAN.

This article examines the concept of surface invariance in dynamical systems from the perspective of recent advancements in the field. Specifically, we draw upon the principles from fractional dynamics and the method of surface analysis introduced by Teixeira. By utilizing a approach that combines these ideas, we explore the existence of surfaces that remain unchanged throughout a dynamical process. However, we also identify instances where such surfaces do not exist, even when there are compact surfaces that contain the system's equilibrium point. The addition of certain conditions is then found to guarantee the presence of surfaces that remain invariant. Moreover, we analyze the specific case of fractional systems in detail. The paper also presents an example to illustrate the application of these results. In the course of this analysis, we draw upon tools from fractional calculus, dynamical systems, and surface theory. The interstellar medium is home to many components that interfere with the reception of signals from pulsars, causing their brightness to change randomly. By studying these changes, researchers can gain a better understanding of the medium and its structure. In a previous study, researchers found similar patterns of change in the brightness of the pulsar B1133+16, indicating that the patterns originated from different places in the interstellar space along the path the signals travel from the pulsar to Earth. In this paper, a mathematical model is used to interpret the data and determine the locations of these places, revealing that the pattern of change that occurs most quickly likely resides within a cloud of gas and dust near the Sun, and the other patterns likely reside further away from the Sun, possibly within a region that includes a large wall of gas and dust that obstructs the view of the pulsar. Additionally, the time it takes for the signals to travel from the pulsar to Earth can be determined, which is 11.73 years, and this time is referred to as the light travel time or pulse period. This knowledge allows for comparing the data collected over different time periods, which reveals that the places where the patterns of change in the brightness of the pulsar originate have changed slightly, possibly due to the motion of the gas and dust in the interstellar space over time. This movement can be calculated to be about 0.0004 kilometers per second, which is very slow. This research relied on analyzing the random changes in the brightness of the pulsar B1133+16 over time and space, which can be applied to other pulsars that experience similar changes, allowing for a deeper understanding of the structure and movement of the interstellar medium and its effect on the signals from these pulsars. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through diluted convolution layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an entirely autoregressive approach with convolutional neural networks. However, its lack of filter sharing leads to pitch control difficulties, particularly when modeling periodic signal components for inputs with large frequency ranges. To overcome this challenge, QPNet adopts a pitch-sensitive diluted convolution architecture with reconfiguration allowing for seamless adaptation to varying signal periods, achieved through a learned probability distribution that determines periodic filter banks. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated across four datasets, including synthetic data with broad frequency ranges and real-world recordings featuring vocal performances. Experimental results show that QPNet yields superior sample efficiency and better generalization capabilities compared to WN, alongside notable improvements in model size without compromising generation quality. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/Parandoss69/QPNet.

For individuals who are deaf or hard-of-hearing, auditory filters can significantly boost the effectiveness of audio-to-text transcription tools like speech recognition systems. To enhance the target speech signal while reducing background noise and unwanted audio, a customized auditory filter can be applied, drawing on the psychological principles of human auditory processing. In this research, we develop an automated methodology to fine-tune these filters, leveraging a hybrid technique that combines unsupervised contrastive learning and conventional optimization methods. The proposed method includes two key innovations: (1) we use unpaired data to train the filters, eliminating the need for labeled training data, and (2) we use a hybrid technique to update the filters, combining both batch and stochastic optimization methods. When combining our proposed filter localization with state-of-the-art speech enhancement techniques, it results in a significant improvement of 1.85 in SI-DRR scores compared to baseline techniques. Moreover, our proposed method outperforms alternative challenges in sound localization tasks, achieving a 4.78 improvement in the mean opinion score (MOS) and a 1.85 improvement in SI-DRR scores. The findings of this research have been demonstrated through comprehensive audio demonstration files available online. The developed methodology has been made available on GitHub for public use. Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by their application in representing complex interactions and relationships between entities in multi-agent scenarios, including areas like social network analysis and hyperparameter optimization. Despite the significant performance of these networks, researchers have expressed concerns about their reliability due to the potential for metric distortions in the learned graph embeddings. In response, researchers have been exploring various methods to impose non-metric constraints on GNNs, such as implementing unique identities for individual nodes and establishing distinct connections between nodes. However, these techniques require large amounts of data for their effective use in various tasks, such as classification and optimization. In contrast to these methods, we present a novel GNN architecture called Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks that seamlessly integrates the Lorentzian metric tensor directly into the network's core, enabling efficient learning of node embeddings under non-euclidean distances while minimizing data requirements. In our experiments, this architecture demonstrates superior performance in various tasks while maintaining a small number of model parameters. We also showcase its versatility by applying it to a wide range of scenarios, from simple linear regression to complex multi-agent analysis, and validate its reliability through rigorous robustness testing. By combining affordable learning with robust node embeddings, Lorentzian GNNs offer a scalable and versatile solution for a broad spectrum of applications involving hyperparameter optimization, classification, and network analysis. This approach provides a foundational layer for various variants, such as hyperdimensional computing, that can be explored in future research. We make the code for Lorentzian GNNs available open-source on GitHub. In our analysis, we found that this architecture thrives in scenarios where the underlying data topology is complex and node connections vary significantly, resulting in distorted Euclidean embeddings. In such cases, Lorentzian GNNs successfully recover the underlying non-euclidean geometry of the data, as demonstrated in our experiments. We also introduce a novel evaluation metric called the geodesic accuracy that allows for precise assessment of the recovery of non-euclidean geometry in these scenarios. This metric can be used to validate the performance of Lorentzian GNNs as well as other similar GNN architectures that learn non-euclidean node embeddings. Our findings with Lorentzian GNNs have implications for various areas, including hyperdimensional computing, psychophysics, and network analysis, and provide a foundation for future research and extensions of this architecture. Reconstructing acoustic structures and their attached components from recorded sound waves is a complex problem with many possible solutions. However, distinguishing between valid combinations of structures and components is difficult because there are often numerous possible acoustic structures and many ways to attach components to them. In addition to this challenge, the problem becomes even more complex when the sound waves are recorded in a three-dimensional space, making it essential to demonstrate that the inferred structure and components are unique when using two-dimensional recordings. This study assumes a simple acoustic structure and aims to invite researchers to take on the inverse challenge of identifying its form from recorded sound waves generated by a vibrating component attached to it. A synthetic example using two-dimensional recordings in a large, open space is provided to facilitate this challenge. When completed, the task will be used to evaluate the proposed optimization-based inversion method presented in the companion paper. All data and methods used in this study are available for others to use. The proposed inversion method and the challenge problem described in this paper were both created by the research group at the University of Michigan, and similar problems are likely to be challenging but also feasible for other research groups to solve. The research was funded by the Office of Naval Research and the National Science Foundation. The findings were published in the journal Applied Mathematical Modeling and the optimization-based inversion method was published in the journal Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering. The research has the reference number ARF-1701-RT-FR-001 and the contract number is N00014-18-1-2651 and the grant number is DGE-1255294 and the grant number is N00014-18-1-2670. The collaborators who contributed to the research, Dr. Song-Qing Shi, Dr. Liang-Yu Niu, and Dr. Liang Zhang, developed the inversion method and challenging problem described in this paper. They created a synthetic example with a specific type of structure and component, then recorded the sound waves generated by the component vibrating at different frequencies from different distances, and finally combined the recorded sound waves with noise to make the challenge more realistic. The collaboration with them facilitated understanding how the accuracy of the inferred structure and components changes when the recorded sound waves contain different levels of noise, and how the accuracy is affected by different frequencies and distances from which the sound waves are recorded. The research was focused on a simple acoustic structure and component, but similar challenges and inversion methods are likely to be feasible for more complex structures and components. The collaboration with any research group is open to creating a challenge problem

In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for describing delayed reciprocal phenomena in complex systems using a novel approach. We demonstrate that this framework's exponential delay function can be modified to better suit observed data, and that this adaptation leads to the Tsallis exponential function when considering time delays. The Tsallis exponential function has been successfully applied to describe power-law distributions in complex systems, citing the example of financial fluctuations. Additionally, we find that the average of this function is comparable to the average of the natural exponential function, which has implications for understanding systemic stability and average return rates in economic systems. The Tsallis exponential function's power-law characteristics also enable us to define a specialized complexity measure, which can be utilized to investigate the intricacy of financial fluctuations. By utilizing random walk models as proxies for these fluctuations, we are able to delve into the underlying mechanics of financial systems and gauge the effect of different market scenarios on system stability. The latter part of the paper is devoted to examining statistically the applicability of the Tsallis exponential function to real-world financial data, comprising stock market return rates and financial network distribution ratios. The findings presented herein demonstrate that the Tsallis exponential function provides a precise statistical fit to financial return rate distributions, the accuracy of which remains evident even when the systems under investigation are in a state of crisis. The opposite holds true for random walk models based on power-law distributions, which lose statistical precision in turbulent times. The Tsallis exponential function's complexity measure is initially found to be indicative of increasing financial system complexity over time, the drivers of which are scrutinized through random walk models. However, during times of financial distress, this complexity is found to suddenly and significantly increase complexitiy, the underlying causes of which are explored in detail. The paper concludes by analyzing the appropriateness of the Tsallis exponential function for modeling delayed reciprocal phenomena, presenting a novel perspective on the underlying mechanics of complex systems based on time-delayed processes, and proposing random walk models as tools for investigating the intricate dynamics of such systems. The findings related to financial fluctuations are the subject of a subsequent publication. The Tsallis exponential function's potential applications extend beyond financial fluctuations to any complex system that can be described using power-law distributions, offering a novel perspective on time-delayed processes and random walk models that may also be applicable to other disciplines that study delayed reciprocal phenomena, as illustrated in Figure 4. The paper is accompanied by three appendices that provide additional information on the Tsallis exponential function, the complexity measure based on power-law distributions, and the random walk models used

This leads to an analysis of the harmonic gauge fixings in (2+1) dimensional gravity, providing a clear understanding of the gauge fixed gravity sector. Our study reveals a complex picture of the harmonic gauge fixings, with multiple solutions arising from the interplay of gravitational waves with cosmological constant dominated spacetimes. This research also clarifies confusing aspects of harmonic gauge fixings mentioned in the literature. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the Banados-Henneaux gauge fixed gravity sector and the harmonic gauge fixings, which involves a gauge transformation that has been previously unreported. This involves a gauge transformation that has gravitational wave components transforming via a non-trivial Sp(2) $R$-matrix, which has a significant impact on the general principles of gauge theory. This result has implications for the fundamental character of the Sp(2) conformal group in the context of (2+1) dimensional gravity. This issue has been previously unexplored in the context of (2+1) dimensional gravity. Our findings demonstrate that the imposition of the harmonic gauge condition on gravitational waves in asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes leads to the imposition of restrictions on the spacetime topology. This involves the requirement that the spacetime must be two-dimensional for the harmonic gauge condition to be imposed on gravitational waves without being disrupted. This condition can be influenced by the behaviour of the gravitational field near the event horizon of black holes. This has implications for the character of the Sp(2) conformal group in the context of (2+1) dimensional gravity, providing a means of determining the effective spacetime dimensions in the presence of a negative cosmological constant. This allows for the derivation of a formula for the relationship between the radius of the event horizon and the scale of the spacetime's curvature. This formula cannot be obtained from the Banados-Henneaux gauge fixed gravity sector alone. This research provides a novel contribution to the general principles of the Sp(2) conformal group in the context of (2+1) dimensional gravity, extending beyond the specific case of anti-de Sitter spacetimes. This research paper looks at a specific variant of rational symplectic geometry called relative rational symplectic geometry, and it proves that two variants, with either constant or linear boundary conditions, are equivalent to a specific variation of Lagrangian cycles. A key tool in this proof is a variant of the Witten conjecture from 2001, which states that two versions of quantum cohomology are also equivalent. Both of these generalizations can be applied to a specific subring called the maximal Frobenius ring, which is derived from a given Lie algebra called the homotopy Lie algebra. The safety of radiology technicians relies on proper infection control measures to prevent them from contracting transmissible diseases from patients. To minimize risk, employers are considering remote imaging interpretation. However, this approach requires radiologists to have access to high-quality images for clear diagnosis. In this work, a novel algorithm is developed to improve the clarity of radiograms in a remote setting, without the need for digital enhancement tools. The proposed method, called Ring Noise Reduction, aims to preserve the original image information while removing noise from radiograms. This method has several key features, including a circle detection mechanism, an image segmentation algorithm, and a region-of-interest (ROI) based removal strategy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively reduces noise and NIST NEMA NEMA images, without NEMA labels, allow for assessment of image clarity. To evaluate the clinical effectiveness of this method, a simple convolutional neural network (CNN) is trained on noise-reduced images and shows a moderate improvement in diagnostic accuracy. ViDaExpert is an application programmed in Java for visualizing, verifying data, and examining multivariate data sets. This instrument is designed to be user-friendly, taking into account the needs of both novice and seasoned data analysts. ViDaExpert enables the creation of nonlinear methods for analyzing high-dimensional data and provides pre-built techniques that can be applied directly. The application features an intuitive graphical interface that allows users to easily navigate and customize visualizations. It supports data sets containing up to nine dimensions and incorporates a straightforward, point-and-click approach for setting up and adjusting methods. ViDaExpert is particularly well-suited for verifying data preprocessing steps, examining the results of nonlinear methods, and visualizing high-dimensional data sets. The application is platform-independent and can be run on Windows, Linux, and Mac operating systems. It is an open-source tool available for free download. The ViDaExpert instrument is a natural progression of its predecessor, ViDa, and represents a significant improvement, incorporating numerous enhancements and new features.
